Additional data files and statistical comments:

The experiments as presented are performed rigorously, with appropriate statistical analysis, however the conclusions that could be drawn are limited and insufficiently novel.

Evaluation of the paper after the first round of revision:

Thank you for submitting your article "Human pancreatic cancer cell exosomes, but not human normal cell exosomes, act as an initiator in cell transformation" for consideration by eLife.

While you have performed a few additional experiments that strengthen the manuscript, the reviewers agree that many of the original criticisms remain unaddressed. As you are aware, in this eLife trial we are committed to ultimately publishing the paper should you choose to proceed with it. However, all of the reviewer and editorial concerns about the validity of these findings will be published in parallel with the paper.

There remain several major areas of concern:

1) The methods used to isolate the exosomes.

Randy Schekman specifically commented upon the new data as follows:

"I have examined the additional data relevant to the concern I raised about the crude fraction they use to claim an exosome activity. As far as I can tell this consists of one data point with a peak fraction of buoyant membranes assayed at one concentration. This would not pass muster by any standard biochemical analysis. I recommend assays across the peak fraction of exosomal marker proteins and a quantitative titration of activity vs. protein concentration in the peak fraction in comparison to the crude starting material. The expectation is that if this activity tracks with exosomes, the specific activity in their biological assay should have been enriched by the buoyant density separation. Without this it is premature to conclude that the activity is associated with exosomes."

2) The notion that exosomes are initiators.

Several of the reviewers raised concerns about using 3T3 cells as the sole evidence of initiation activity. This was not addressed experimentally, but instead the authors state that "It will be very interesting to test this function in other cell types, and will be done in future studies." Despite this being a major concern, this is still left unaddressed.

Why this is important is related to the new data in Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, they show that the background foci actually do form tumors, albeit at a slower rate and with lower efficiency than the exosome treated 3T3 foci. But the fact that the background foci do indeed form tumors actually argues against a pure initiator activity – it seems to accelerate what is already happening in the background foci anyway. Thus, a central argument that these exosomes are true initiators does not seem fully accurate. In the absence of other cell types other than 3T3s, it is hard to state this definitively outside of this one context.

3) The proteomic analysis.

While the authors make it clear how they performed the analysis, it is still confusing to state "However, proteins found in transformed cells shown in Figure 4 exhibit more divergence from control cells" Divergence based on what statistical measure? Venn diagrams are not statistical methods, and it is not clear that the PANTHER data shows true statistical enrichment in the exosome treated cells.

4) Exome analysis.

In the rebuttal, the authors state that "we feel confident that the method we used is sufficient to obtain reliable results". Yet the request to analyze this data with additional pipelines and more stringent statistics was not performed. There is no orthogonal validation of this pipeline to ensure that the results are accurate.

In looking at their more detailed methods, it is now clear that they are comparing their exomes to the human reference genomes (GRCm38), so that the variants being called are actually just variants that differ from this reference genome, and not the parental 3T3 cells. How do you know that most of the called variants are not just called SNPs or baseline point mutations between 3T3 cells and the human reference genome? Why not compare the exome data to the parental 3T3 cells rather than the human reference genome?

The authors now provide additional data, using the same pipelines, on bulk exome data on both untreated and TPA treated foci in Figures 5 and 6. In Figure 5—figure supplement 1, they essentially show that the number of mutations in the untreated or TPA treated cells is similar to that in the MCA/TPA or ExC/TPA foci. But if the basic idea is that exosomes act as initiators through increases in mutation rate, then why are the number of mutations essentially the same. Furthermore, in the data in Figure 6, you show that the signature 20 is higher in the MCA/TPA or ExC/TPA samples compared to untreated/TPA, but this just looks like a modest increase, and there is no statistical analysis to say whether these are really different. How do you confirm that you are really enriching for this signature in this dataset other than a heatmap which looks to be so.

Finally, it is not clear that bulk sequencing of this population of highly mutated cells is appropriate. If we consider that each cell could have many different mutations, the more appropriate experiment is to create single cell clones out of the transformed foci, let that grow up, and then perform the exome analysis on these isolated clones. While this is an expensive and ultimately very time consuming method, it would ultimately be much more informative in understanding how the mutations occur in each cell, rather than a population of cells which may or may not have defects is mismatch repair.

5) The role of mismatch repair.

While we recognize that adding in single mismatch repair genes may not rescue the phenotypes, at the same time the authors are making a very bold claim that exosomes specifically lead to MMR defects. This is perhaps the most intriguing idea in the paper, but without any experiments to mechanistically dissect this it remains correlative.

Evaluation of the paper after the second round of revision:

In this revised manuscript, the authors have tried to address several of the issues brought up during the review process. As part of this trial, we will proceed with publication of the manuscript although we do feel several issues remain unresolved that could have further strengthened the paper.

First, Dr Schekman raised a point that dose response relationships comparing the more purified exosomes with the crude starting material would be required to establish that the buoyant density gradient achieved purification of the active vesicle species. The single concentration of the gradient fraction used in the new version of the paper fails to establish meaningful purification.

Second, while we agree that the 3T3 assay is a standard initiator assay, the development of other assays to confirm this potentially new and important function of exosomes would have provided significant confidence that this is a generalizable activity.

Third, the authors have used one informatic pipeline for their analysis, whereas adding in additional and complementary pipelines for mutation calling (i.e MuTect, etc) would have provided increased confidence that these are reproducible results from an informatic standpoint. Analysis of single cell clones from the transformed cells would have also given a more fine-grained analysis of the mutational pattern induced via exosomes, which cannot be achieved by bulk sequencing alone.

claims.claim: Haploinsufficiency of MMR genes may occur where responding to DNA damage requires a higher dosage of MMR protein than the repair function.
claims.source: Haploinsufficiency may be function-specific; for example, it has been demonstrated that responding to DNA damage requires a higher dosage of MMR protein than the repair function (Peltomäki, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about MMR gene function supported by citation to prior literature.

results.result: Exosomes isolated from pancreatic cancer cells were characterized and validated using multiple methods including western blot, mass spectrometry, TEM, and NTA, confirming the presence of exosomal markers and appropriate size distribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C19 and C30-C31 collectively demonstrate rigorous characterization of exosomes using orthogonal methods (western blot, mass spectrometry, TEM, NTA). The data show presence of expected markers (CD63, Alix, TSG101), absence of contaminants (Calnexin, α-actinin, HSP90), appropriate morphology, and size distribution consistent with exosomes. Both crude and purified preparations were characterized.

results.result: Pancreatic cancer cell exosomes, but not normal cell exosomes, can act as an initiator in the two-stage cell transformation assay when combined with the promoter TPA, resulting in increased foci formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C22-C29 demonstrate that exosomes from four different pancreatic cancer cell lines (including both KRAS mutant and wild-type) can initiate transformation when combined with TPA, while exosomes from normal cells (HPDE, fibroblasts) cannot. The data show statistically significant increases in foci formation (3-4 foci/well) above background levels (1 foci/well) for cancer cell exosomes but not normal cell exosomes.

results.result: Cancer cell exosomes cannot transform cells when used alone or as a promoter in the cell transformation assay.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 and C90-C91 demonstrate that cancer cell exosomes used alone (throughout the entire assay) or as a promoter (after MCA initiation) result in only background levels of foci formation. This establishes that exosomes specifically function as initiators, not as complete transforming agents or promoters.

results.result: Purified exosomes retain initiator activity, which requires intact vesicles and a minimum concentration of 8 ng/mL protein.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 and C97-C99 demonstrate that sucrose gradient-purified exosomes retain initiator activity, establishing that the activity is not due to contaminants. Dose-response studies show activity at ≥8 ng/mL, and boiling exosomes (which destroys membrane integrity) eliminates activity, demonstrating that intact vesicles are required.

results.result: Cancer cell exosomes function as classic initiators by working with multiple promoters (TPA and CdCl2) to induce cell transformation.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37, C100, and C137 demonstrate that cancer cell exosomes can initiate transformation with two different promoters (TPA and CdCl2), a defining characteristic of classic initiators. CdCl2 alone produces only background foci, confirming the requirement for both initiation and promotion.

results.result: Cells transformed by cancer cell exosome initiation form tumors when injected into immunocompromised mice, confirming their malignant phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C38-C43, C102-C107 demonstrate that cells from both MCA/TPA and cancer cell exosome/TPA transformed foci form tumors in mice at multiple cell concentrations, while non-transformed control cells do not. Tumor growth correlates with cell number injected, and histological analysis confirms fibrosarcomas, consistent with the mesenchymal origin of NIH/3T3 cells.

results.result: Background foci from untreated cells occasionally form tumors in mice, but these grow later and more slowly than transformed foci.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45 show that 6 of 15 mice injected with untreated background foci developed tumors, but these grew significantly later and slower than tumors from initiator/promoter-treated cells. This observation is consistent with prior literature and demonstrates the distinction between spontaneous and induced transformation.

results.result: Proteomic analysis of cells treated with initiators (MCA or cancer cell exosomes) shows no marked global changes compared to untreated cells, potentially because random changes occur in specific proteins among specific cells in the population.
results.evaluation: Claim C46 demonstrates no detectable global proteomic changes after initiator treatment, but claims C109-C112 provide only speculative explanations for this observation. The lack of detectable changes could reflect technical limitations of bulk analysis, true absence of changes, or the proposed random distribution of changes across the cell population. Additional single-cell or targeted analyses would be needed to distinguish these possibilities.

results.result: Proteomic analysis of transformed foci reveals major changes compared to control cells, with common proteins showing high overlap between foci of the same type but unique proteins showing little overlap.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48, C108, and C113 demonstrate that >1500 proteins were identified in transformed foci, with common proteins (present in both control and transformed cells) showing high overlap between foci of the same type, while unique proteins (absent in controls) show little overlap. GO enrichment analysis reveals multiple enriched molecular functions, indicating major proteomic changes in transformed cells.

results.result: Exome sequencing reveals that transformed foci cluster together by PCA and share similar mutational profiles despite originating from independent mutagenic events with unique variants.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 and C114 demonstrate that the six transformed foci (MCA/TPA and ExC/TPA) cluster together when compared to background foci, but show no clear relationship when analyzed alone, consistent with independent origins. The diversity in specific variants combined with clustering by mutational signatures supports the conclusion that each foci arose from distinct mutagenic events.

results.result: Transformed foci share COSMIC Signatures 20 and 15 (associated with defective mismatch repair) as top contributors, while background foci show COSMIC Signature 3 (associated with double-strand break repair failure) as the top signature.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54, C115-C116 demonstrate clear differences in mutational signatures between transformed and background foci. All six transformed foci show COSMIC Signatures 20 and 15 as top contributors, both associated with MMR defects, while background foci show COSMIC Signature 3 as the top signature. This distinction is well-supported by the MutaGene analysis shown in Figure 6.

results.result: Each transformed foci contains unique missense mutations in mismatch repair genes that are predicted to be deleterious, with wild-type alleles still present, while background foci lack such mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58, C117, C120-C121, and C140 demonstrate that all six transformed foci contain missense mutations in MMR genes, but each foci has unique mutations. In silico analysis predicts these mutations are deleterious. Wild-type alleles remain present, and none of the untreated background foci (and only one TPA-only foci) had MMR gene mutations. This supports the conclusion that MMR dysfunction drives transformation.

results.result: Analysis of oncogene mutations across the 12 foci samples reveals very few shared mutations and no common point mutations, indicating no likely driver mutation in classical oncogenes.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60 demonstrate that analysis of 190 known oncogenes revealed very few shared mutations between independent foci of the same type and no common point mutations across samples. This negative result is important as it suggests transformation is not driven by classical oncogene mutations but rather by MMR dysfunction.

results.result: Cancer cell exosomes act as initiators by inducing random mutations in recipient cells, creating a pool of randomly mutated cells from which the promoter TPA drives transformation through a non-random molecular path toward mismatch repair dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6 and C61 state that exosomes induce random mutations, supported by the diversity of variants observed. However, claims C65-C67 propose that TPA drives a non-random path toward MMR dysfunction, which is speculative. While the convergence on COSMIC Signatures 20/15 across all transformed foci is striking and well-documented (C51-C52), the mechanistic explanation for how TPA selects for MMR-deficient cells from a randomly mutated population requires additional experimental validation. The proposal is logical but remains inferential.

results.result: Haploinsufficiency of MMR genes may be function-specific, with DNA damage response requiring higher MMR protein levels than repair function.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C119 and C141 cite established knowledge from prior literature (Peltomäki, 2016) that MMR gene haploinsufficiency can be function-specific. This is used to explain how the presence of wild-type alleles in transformed foci may still result in MMR dysfunction. The claim is well-supported by citation to prior work.

results.result: Background foci show COSMIC Signature 3 as the main driver, associated with double-strand break repair failure, which likely contributes to the high number of variants observed in these samples.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C124 demonstrate that all six background foci show COSMIC Signature 3 as the top signature, associated with homologous recombination defects. The logical inference that this contributes to the high variant count is reasonable given the known association of this signature with genomic instability.

results.result: The findings raise the possibility that exosomes secreted by primary tumors could orchestrate independent transformation events within tumors, potentially explaining genetically unrelated cells observed in some PDAC patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 and C126 connect the current findings to prior observations of genetically unrelated IPMNs in PDAC patients (Felsenstein et al., 2018) and speculate that exosomes could mediate independent transformation events in vivo. While this is an interesting hypothesis consistent with the data, it remains speculative and would require additional studies in more relevant cell types and in vivo models to validate.

results.result: The initiator activity of pancreatic cancer cell exosomes is independent of KRAS mutation status and is a trait unique to cancer cell exosomes, not normal cell exosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73, C92, and C136 demonstrate that exosomes from both KRAS mutant (Capan-2, MIA PaCa-2, Panc-1) and wild-type (BxPC-3) cancer cell lines can initiate transformation, while exosomes from normal cells (HPDE, fibroblasts) cannot. This establishes that the initiator activity is a general property of cancer cell exosomes independent of specific oncogenic mutations.

results.result: The two-stage cell transformation assay requires both an initiator and promoter to observe increased transformation above background levels, with MCA/TPA treatment resulting in 3-4 foci/well compared to 1 foci/well background.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C21 and C89 establish the baseline performance of the CTA with chemical initiator (MCA) and promoter (TPA). The requirement for both components and the quantitative difference between treated (3-4 foci/well) and background (1 foci/well) conditions are well-demonstrated and consistent with prior literature.

results.result: Additional studies are needed to understand the molecular mechanism of cancer cell exosome-mediated initiation, particularly in more relevant cell types such as human epithelial cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C128 and C112 acknowledge limitations of the current study and identify important future directions. The use of mouse NIH/3T3 cells with human exosomes, while justified by conserved molecular functions, represents a limitation. Testing in human epithelial cells would be more relevant for understanding pancreatic cancer biology.
